book_title: Momma May Be Mad: A Memoir
subject_line: Proving the psychiatrist wrong in Momma May Be Mad
email_body:
Dear Kerry,

I read about Momma May Be Mad and its nonlinear way of reconstructing years of bipolar disorder, anorexia and alcoholism while raising young children, including the psychiatrist who once called you "hopeless." Congratulations on the Georgia Author of the Year award for memoir. I would love to ask how you decided on the book's broken chronology, and whether that structure came from memory itself or from revision.

subject_line: The San Francisco to Syracuse drive in Off the Books
email_body:
Dear Soma,

Off the Books caught my attention for its road: Mei, a Dartmouth dropout driving a limo off the books, taking Henry and his large black suitcase from San Francisco all the way to Syracuse, one leg per chapter. Since you now teach at SUNY Oswego, not far from where that drive ends, I would like to ask how the geography of the trip took shape, and how you paced the moral stakes across each stop.

subject_line: From Liliana in Boston to Maya in Guatemala
email_body:
Dear Jennifer,

Your two YA novels seem to face each other across a border: Liliana Cruz in Don't Ask Me Where I'm From, a first-generation teen in Boston reinventing herself at a wealthy, mostly white school, and Maya in Borderless, who loved her life as a design student in Guatemala. I would be curious to ask what it was like to move the center of gravity from a Boston classroom to Guatemala, and how teaching at Framingham State shapes the young readers you imagine.

book_title: All Skate: True Tales from Middle Life
subject_line: All Skate and the things you can't forget
email_body:
Dear Lori,

Looking through your books, from the flight-attendant years of Miss New York Has Everything to They Write Your Name on a Grain of Rice, where cancer becomes a frame for living even so, I noticed how often you return to Pittsburgh and to caregiving. With All Skate: True Tales from Middle Life out from Roadside Press and a memoir in verse announced for 2026, I would like to ask how middle age changed what you think a true tale owes its reader.

book_title: The Quickening: Motherhood, Antarctica and Cultivating Hope in a Warming World
subject_line: Carrying the question of motherhood to Antarctica
email_body:
Dear Elizabeth,

The Quickening sets two decisions side by side: whether to have a child in a warming world, and what you witnessed on the voyage to Antarctica that the book documents. After Rising: Dispatches from the New American Shore stayed close to eroding coastlines, I would like to ask how it felt to write from somewhere so remote, and whether the hope in the subtitle came before the journey or out of it.

book_title: A Literary Guide to Washington, DC
subject_line: Walking Washington's literary past, and its cemeteries
email_body:
Dear Kim,

A Literary Guide to Washington, DC builds four walking tours around the writers who lived in the capital, and By Broad Potomac's Shore gathers 132 poets active there before about 1930. Now that your cemetery walking-tour book with Rivanna Books is underway, I would like to ask what changes when the literary map you are drawing moves from writers' houses to their graves, and how that research sits alongside Q&A for the End of the World, your poems with Michael Gushue.

subject_line: Marvin Gaye, Nipsey Hussle and a sibling in Come Kingdom
email_body:
Dear Derrick,

Come Kingdom follows a speaker and his partner trying to give their son a sibling, while the poems call on Marvin Gaye, Whitney Houston, Tupac Shakur and Nipsey Hussle. In your LSU Press essay, "The Two Lives of Derrick Harriell," you write about where the book came from, and I would like to ask how those musicians entered such a private story about wanting to become parents again, and whether they arrived early or late in the writing.

subject_line: The pocket worlds of Time's Agent
email_body:
Dear Brenda,

Time's Agent moved from the stories of The Rock Eaters into a novella of love, loss, time travel and robots, and USF's write-up describes how its pocket worlds reveal deeper truths, an approach that earned it a Philip K. Dick Award. I would like to ask how you decide when a speculative idea needs the longer arc of a novella rather than a story, and what the pocket worlds let you say that realism could not.

subject_line: From Happy Like This to How to Care for a Human Girl
email_body:
Dear Ashley,

You moved from Happy Like This, the story collection that won the 2019 John Simmons Short Fiction Award, to a novel whose title, How to Care for a Human Girl, reads almost like a manual. I would like to ask what that shift from short fiction to a novel asked of you, whether the title came early or late, and how teaching creative writing at the University of Montevallo feeds the way you build a book.
